title: Frontend Systems — a field guide
subtitle: 15 frontend performance & architecture topics across three tiers — from first principles to system-design depth, each with the what, how & why, real references, diagrams, case studies, and questions to test yourself.

tiers.name: Loading & Delivery
tiers.blurb: How a page gets from network bytes to visible pixels — the rendering pipeline, the metrics that grade it, and the caching/loading techniques that make it fast.

topics.name: Critical Rendering Path
topics.premise: The Critical Rendering Path (CRP) is the sequence of steps the browser performs to turn the bytes of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into pixels on screen: parse HTML into the DOM, parse CSS into the CSSOM, combine them into a render tree, run layout to compute geometry, paint pixels into layers, and composite those layers to the display. Understanding the CRP means understanding exactly which resources the browser must have in hand before it can paint the first pixel, and how each resource can block or unblock that first paint.
topics.year: The pipeline model was popularized by Google's 'Critical Rendering Path' guidance around 2014 (Ilya Grigorik's web performance work), but it describes browser-engine behavior that predates it. The stages map onto the rendering pipelines of Blink/WebKit and Gecko. Modern refinements — the compositor thread, GPU rasterization, and metrics like First Contentful Paint / Largest Contentful Paint — were formalized through the W3C Paint Timing and Element Timing specs (2017 onward) and web.dev guidance.
topics.why: A browser cannot paint text or boxes until it knows two things: what the structure of the page is (the DOM tree) and how each node should look (computed styles from the CSSOM). These are produced by two independent parsers reading two independent resource types, so the first paint is gated on the slower of the two. HTML parsing is incremental and streaming, but it stops dead when it hits a synchronous <script> because that script might call document.write or read/modify the DOM — so the parser cannot safely continue (JS is parser-blocking). CSS is render-blocking because applying a stylesheet later could restyle everything already on screen, producing a flash of unstyled then styled content; to avoid that, the browser refuses to construct the render tree until the CSSOM is complete. Every byte on the critical path is latency the user waits through before seeing anything, and network round-trips dominate, so the game is minimizing the number, size, and dependency depth of critical resources.
solutions: DOM construction (tokenize → tree)

The HTML parser converts bytes → characters (per the declared/detected encoding) → tokens → nodes → the DOM tree. It is incremental and streaming, so the browser can start building structure before the full document arrives — but it pauses on parser-blocking scripts.
CSSOM construction

CSS is parsed into the CSS Object Model, a tree of computed style rules. Unlike the DOM, CSS is not render-incremental: partial CSS could be overridden by later rules, so the browser treats every stylesheet in <head> as render-blocking and waits for the full CSSOM before building the render tree.
Render tree, layout (reflow), paint

The render tree merges DOM + CSSOM, keeping only visible nodes (display:none is excluded, visibility:hidden is kept). Layout/reflow computes exact box geometry (position and size) in the viewport; paint fills pixels — text, colors, borders, shadows, images — into paint records, typically across multiple layers.
Composite

Painted layers are handed to the compositor, which assembles them into the final frame, often on a separate thread and the GPU. transform and opacity animations can be run purely on the compositor, skipping layout and paint entirely — which is why they are the cheap properties to animate.
defer and async on scripts

A plain <script> is parser-blocking and executes in order. `defer` downloads in parallel and runs after the DOM is parsed, in document order — ideal for app code that touches the DOM. `async` downloads in parallel and executes as soon as it arrives, out of order — suitable for independent third-party scripts. Both remove the parser block.
Inline critical CSS, defer the rest

Inline the small amount of CSS needed to style above-the-fold content directly in the <head> so first paint needs no extra round-trip, then load the full stylesheet non-blockingly (e.g. rel=preload swapped to rel=stylesheet, or media-toggling). This shrinks the render-blocking CSS to the minimum.
preload / preconnect resource hints

<link rel=preload> tells the browser to fetch a late-discovered critical resource (a font, a hero image, an imported CSS) early, before the parser would otherwise find it. <link rel=preconnect> warms the TCP+TLS connection to a critical origin so the round-trips are already paid for when the request fires.
Minimize and reduce critical resources

Fewer critical bytes and fewer critical round-trips = faster first paint. Minify and compress CSS/JS, split off non-critical code, mark stylesheets that only apply to print or other media (which makes them non-render-blocking), and avoid deep request chains where one critical resource discovers another.
topics.papers: Google/Ilya Grigorik, 'Constructing the Object Model' and 'Render-Tree Construction, Layout, and Paint' (web.dev / Web Fundamentals). The HTML parsing model is normatively defined by the WHATWG HTML Standard (section 'Parsing HTML documents'), including the exact rules for parser-blocking scripts, `async`, and `defer`. CSS render-blocking behavior follows from the CSSOM and CSS Cascade specifications. Paint/element timing metrics come from the W3C Paint Timing and Element Timing specifications.
topics.takeaway: The browser cannot paint until it has both a DOM and a complete CSSOM; CSS is render-blocking and synchronous JS is parser-blocking, so the entire optimization game is shrinking the number, size, and dependency depth of resources on that critical path before first paint.
topics.deepDive:
Start from what the browser physically needs before it can draw a single meaningful pixel. To lay out and paint any element it must know (a) that the element exists and where it sits in the tree — that is the DOM — and (b) what it should look like — its computed style, which comes from the CSSOM. Neither tree alone is enough: the render tree is their intersection. So the time-to-first-paint is bounded below by the time to build both, and because HTML and CSS arrive over the network as separate resources, first paint is gated on the slower of the two dependency chains. This single fact explains almost every CRP optimization technique.

DOM construction is streaming and forgiving: the parser reads bytes as they arrive and grows the tree incrementally, which is why a well-structured HTML document can start rendering before it has fully downloaded. The parser's enemy is the synchronous <script>. When the tokenizer reaches a plain <script src>, it must stop — the script may call document.write, mutate nodes it hasn't seen, or read layout — so the browser blocks parsing, fetches the script, executes it, and only then resumes. Worse, if that script reads a computed style or geometry, it also needs the CSSOM, so a stylesheet in the <head> can transitively block script execution, which blocks parsing. This cascade is why script placement and the async/defer attributes matter so much: defer preserves order and runs after parsing (safe for app code), while async runs whenever it lands (fine for independent analytics, dangerous for order-dependent code).

CSS is render-blocking for a correctness reason, not a performance one. If the browser painted with a half-downloaded stylesheet, a later rule could restyle everything already on screen — a flash of unstyled content. To avoid that, the engine waits for the complete CSSOM before constructing the render tree. The lever here is scoping: a stylesheet with a media attribute that doesn't match the current context (e.g. media=print) is downloaded but not render-blocking, and inlined critical CSS removes the round-trip entirely. This is the basis of the 'inline critical, defer the rest' pattern that frameworks like Next.js and tools like Critters/Beasties automate.

Once the render tree exists, layout (reflow) computes geometry and paint produces pixel-fill records, usually across several compositing layers. Compositing then assembles those layers into a frame — increasingly on a dedicated thread and the GPU. The system-design consequence is a cost hierarchy: changing a property that affects geometry (width, top, font-size) forces layout + paint + composite; changing paint-only properties (color, box-shadow) skips layout; and animating transform or opacity can skip both layout and paint, running entirely on the compositor. That is why 'animate transform/opacity, not top/left' is not folklore — it is a direct consequence of where each property enters the pipeline.

From a frontend system-design angle, the CRP is the substrate under Core Web Vitals. First Contentful Paint and Largest Contentful Paint are literally 'how fast did we get through the critical path for the first / largest content.' Server-side rendering wins because it lets the browser start DOM construction from meaningful HTML immediately instead of waiting for a JS bundle to construct the DOM at runtime; but SSR shifts the bottleneck to hydration, where a large parser-blocking or long-executing bundle can delay interactivity even after paint. Streaming SSR and partial hydration exist precisely to keep the critical path short while deferring the expensive JS.

The failure modes are predictable once you think in dependency chains: a render-blocking web font with no fallback causes invisible text (FOIT); a third-party script in the <head> without async/defer blocks the parser on someone else's server latency; a deep request chain (HTML → CSS → @import another CSS → font) serializes round-trips that could have been parallelized with preload. The mental model to carry into an interview: enumerate every resource on the path to first paint, ask of each 'does it block the parser, block rendering, or neither, and can I make it not block,' then minimize how many such resources exist and how deep their discovery chain is.

caseStudies.title: web.dev: render-blocking CSS and the critical CSS pattern
caseStudies.body: Google's web.dev performance guidance documents that a single external stylesheet referenced in the <head> blocks rendering of the entire page until it downloads and the CSSOM is built, and demonstrates that inlining the styles needed for above-the-fold content while deferring the rest measurably improves First Contentful Paint. Tools such as Critters (and its maintained fork Beasties, used by Angular) and Next.js's built-in critical-CSS handling automate this by extracting the used rules at build time and inlining them, then loading the full sheet non-blockingly.

caseStudies.title: Async vs defer for third-party scripts
caseStudies.body: The WHATWG HTML spec and MDN document that a classic <script> in the <head> without async or defer halts the parser until the script is fetched and executed — a well-documented cause of slow first paint when the script lives on a slow third-party origin. Moving such scripts to defer (or async for independent ones) is the standard, documented remedy: the parser keeps building the DOM in parallel and first paint no longer waits on that network round-trip.

mcqs.q: Why does the browser treat an external stylesheet in the <head> as render-blocking?
options: Because CSS files are always larger than HTML files
Because a partially applied stylesheet could be overridden by later rules, causing incorrect painting, so the render tree waits for the complete CSSOM
Because CSS must be executed like JavaScript before the DOM can be built
Because the DOM cannot be constructed until the CSSOM exists
mcqs.explanation: Correct: CSS is not render-incremental — later rules can restyle earlier ones — so painting with an incomplete CSSOM risks a flash of restyled content. The engine therefore waits for the full CSSOM before building the render tree. Reason from correctness, not size: the DOM is built independently of CSS (options about DOM/CSSOM ordering are wrong), and CSS is declarative, not executed like JS.

mcqs.q: A team adds `defer` to their main application bundle in the <head>. What is the effect?
options: The script executes immediately, blocking the parser
The script is downloaded in parallel and executed after the DOM is parsed, preserving document order
The script is downloaded in parallel and executed the instant it arrives, possibly out of order
The script is not downloaded until the user interacts
mcqs.explanation: defer downloads in parallel without blocking the parser, then runs after DOM construction completes, in document order — the safe choice for app code that depends on the DOM and on ordering. async runs on arrival out of order, suitable only for independent scripts, which is why the out-of-order option is wrong here.

mcqs.q: Which set of steps must complete before the browser can produce its first meaningful frame?
options: DOM only, then paint
CSSOM only, then composite
DOM + CSSOM → render tree → layout → paint → composite
JavaScript execution → DOM → composite
mcqs.explanation: The render tree is the intersection of the DOM and a complete CSSOM; from there the browser runs layout to compute geometry, paints pixels, and composites layers into a frame. First paint is gated on both trees, which is why either a slow stylesheet or a parser-blocking script can delay it.

mcqs.q: You need a smooth 60fps element animation. Which property is cheapest for the browser to animate and why?
options: top / left, because they are simple numeric properties
width / height, because layout is fast for small elements
transform, because it can run on the compositor thread and skip layout and paint
margin, because it does not affect siblings
mcqs.explanation: transform (and opacity) can be handled entirely by the compositor, skipping the layout and paint stages of the pipeline, so they animate cheaply and off the main thread. top/left/width/height/margin all trigger layout (reflow) plus paint every frame, which is why they cause jank.

mcqs.q: A page's first paint is slow because a critical font is discovered late (HTML → CSS → @font-face → font). What is the most direct fix?
options: Add no-store to the font's Cache-Control
<link rel=preload as=font> the font in the <head> so it is fetched early instead of after CSS parses
Switch the font file from woff2 to ttf
Wrap the stylesheet in an async script tag
mcqs.explanation: The problem is a serialized discovery chain: the font is only found after CSS is parsed. rel=preload tells the browser to fetch the late-discovered critical resource early, collapsing the round-trips. no-store would hurt (it prevents caching), ttf is larger than woff2, and stylesheets can't be loaded via a script tag.

topics.name: Core Web Vitals
topics.premise: Core Web Vitals are Google's set of three field-measurable metrics that quantify the real user experience of a web page across three dimensions: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) for loading, Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) for visual stability, and Interaction to Next Paint (INP) for responsiveness. Each has a specific 'good' threshold, and a page is assessed at the 75th percentile of real visits, segmented by device. Because they are part of Google's page-experience signals, they matter for both users and search.
topics.year: Google launched the Web Vitals initiative in May 2020 with LCP, First Input Delay (FID), and CLS. INP was introduced as an experimental responsiveness metric in 2022, promoted to 'pending' in 2023, and on March 12, 2024 it officially replaced FID as the responsiveness Core Web Vital — FID was retired. The metrics are backed by W3C performance specs (Largest Contentful Paint, Layout Instability, Event Timing) and surfaced through the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX).
topics.why: Traditional performance metrics (onload, DOMContentLoaded, total page weight) correlate poorly with what a user actually perceives. A page can fire onload quickly yet still feel slow because the main content painted late, or shifted under the user's finger, or froze when they tapped. Google's insight was to measure user-perceived experience directly at three moments the human nervous system is sensitive to: how long until I see the main thing (loading), does the layout stay put so I don't misclick (stability), and when I interact does the page respond before I notice a lag (responsiveness). These are measured in the field because the same code performs wildly differently across real devices, networks, and CPUs — a fast developer laptop hides the low-end Android reality. Field data captured at the 75th percentile deliberately reflects the experience of the slower quarter of visits rather than a flattering median.
solutions: LCP — Largest Contentful Paint (good ≤ 2.5s)

Time from navigation start until the largest content element in the viewport (often a hero image, video poster, or large text block) is rendered. It approximates 'when did the main content appear.' Driven by server response time (TTFB), render-blocking resources, resource load time, and client-side render delay.
CLS — Cumulative Layout Shift (good ≤ 0.1)

A unitless score summing the largest burst of unexpected layout shifts during the page's lifespan. Each shift = impact fraction (viewport area affected) × distance fraction (how far it moved). Caused by images/ads/iframes without dimensions, injected content, and web fonts that reflow text (FOUT).
INP — Interaction to Next Paint (good ≤ 200ms)

Measures responsiveness across the whole page lifetime by observing all click/tap/keyboard interactions and reporting (roughly) the worst latency: input delay + event-handler processing time + presentation delay until the next frame paints. It replaced FID on March 12, 2024.
The 75th-percentile rule

A page 'passes' a metric only if 75% of real page loads meet the good threshold, evaluated separately for mobile and desktop. This anti-cherry-picking rule ensures the slower quarter of the user population is represented rather than hidden behind an average.
Field data (RUM) vs lab data (synthetic)

Field/RUM (CrUX, web-vitals JS library) reflects real users across real conditions and is the source of truth for the vitals. Lab/synthetic (Lighthouse, WebPageTest) runs in a controlled environment for debugging and regression-catching — but cannot measure INP or CLS's full lifetime because there is no real user interaction; Lighthouse uses Total Blocking Time (TBT) as an INP proxy.
Diagnosing LCP

Break LCP into TTFB, resource load delay, resource load time, and element render delay. Fix by improving server/CDN latency, preloading the LCP image, removing render-blocking CSS/JS, and avoiding lazy-loading the above-the-fold hero.
Diagnosing CLS

Always set width/height (or aspect-ratio) on images, videos, and ad slots; reserve space for injected/embedded content; and preload fonts with font-display swap plus size-matched fallbacks to minimize reflow. Never insert content above existing content unless in response to a user interaction.
Diagnosing INP

Break long tasks so the main thread can respond, yield to the event loop (e.g. scheduler.yield / setTimeout / isInputPending), debounce expensive handlers, avoid large synchronous re-renders, and move heavy work to a web worker. INP is dominated by main-thread contention.
topics.papers: Google web.dev is the canonical source: 'Web Vitals' overview and the individual metric articles (LCP, CLS, INP), plus the March 2024 announcement 'INP is a Core Web Vital'. The underlying definitions are W3C specifications: Largest Contentful Paint, Layout Instability (CLS), and Event Timing (INP/FID). Field data is published via the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX). The open-source `web-vitals` JavaScript library implements the standard measurement in the field.

topics.takeaway: Core Web Vitals measure user-perceived loading (LCP ≤ 2.5s), visual stability (CLS ≤ 0.1), and responsiveness (INP ≤ 200ms) from real users at the 75th percentile — since March 2024 INP replaced FID — so you must fix what the field says, not what a fast lab machine shows.
topics.deepDive:
The first-principles motivation is that classic timing events measure the machine, not the human. onload tells you when the browser finished loading resources, but a user's judgment of 'is this page good' forms at three distinct moments: when the main content becomes visible, whether the layout stays stable enough to read and click, and whether the page reacts when they touch it. Core Web Vitals are three metrics chosen to line up with those three perceptual moments — loading, stability, responsiveness — and each is defined so it can be measured on real users in the wild, not just in a lab.

LCP answers 'when did the main thing show up?' It records the render time of the largest image or text block in the viewport, which is a good proxy for the primary content. The good threshold is 2.5 seconds. The right way to reason about LCP is to decompose it: time-to-first-byte (server + network), then the delay before the LCP resource starts loading, then how long it takes to load, then the render delay after it arrives. Each sub-part has different fixes — a slow TTFB is a backend/CDN problem, a late-discovered hero image is a preload problem, and a render delay is usually render-blocking CSS/JS or client-side hydration. A classic own-goal is lazy-loading the above-the-fold hero image, which pushes LCP later.

CLS answers 'did things move unexpectedly?' It is unitless: for each unexpected shift, the browser multiplies the fraction of the viewport that moved (impact) by how far it moved (distance), and CLS is the largest burst of such shifts (a session window). The good threshold is 0.1. The root cause is always the same physics: the browser reserved no space, so when content arrives it reflows what's already there. Setting explicit width/height or aspect-ratio on media, reserving space for ads and embeds, and handling web fonts carefully (font-display and metric-matched fallbacks) eliminate most of it. The one legitimate exception the metric tolerates is a shift within 500ms of a user interaction, since the user caused it.

INP answers 'when I interact, does it respond?' and it is the subtle one, especially because it replaced FID on March 12, 2024. FID only measured the input delay of the very first interaction — the time before the handler started running — which flattered pages: it ignored how long the handler took and every interaction after the first. INP instead observes all interactions across the page's lifetime and reports (near) the worst full latency: input delay + processing time + presentation delay until the next paint. Because it captures handler execution and rendering, INP is fundamentally a main-thread-contention metric. The good threshold is 200ms. You improve it by breaking up long tasks, yielding to the event loop (scheduler.yield, isInputPending, or setTimeout), avoiding giant synchronous re-renders (a real risk in framework apps), and offloading heavy computation to workers.

The measurement model is as important as the metrics. Vitals are field metrics: the source of truth is real-user monitoring, published by Google in the Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) and measurable in your own analytics via the web-vitals library. They are assessed at the 75th percentile, split by mobile and desktop — meaning a page only passes if three out of four real loads are good, which deliberately surfaces the experience of the slower, low-end-device quarter of your audience. Lab tools (Lighthouse, WebPageTest) are for debugging and CI regression gates, but they run one controlled trace and cannot see real interactions, so Lighthouse cannot compute INP at all and reports Total Blocking Time as a proxy. Treating a green Lighthouse score as 'passing Core Web Vitals' is a common and costly mistake.

For frontend system design, the vitals force architectural choices. SSR/streaming improves LCP by delivering meaningful HTML fast, but a heavy hydration bundle can wreck INP — so partial/progressive hydration and islands architectures exist to keep the main thread free for interaction. A CDN and good caching cut TTFB and thus LCP. Image pipelines (responsive sizes, modern formats, correct dimensions) serve both LCP and CLS. And because the vitals are measured in the field, the correct workflow is closed-loop: ship, measure real users via CrUX/RUM, find the specific offending metric and its sub-part, fix, and re-measure — rather than optimizing to a lab number that a real low-end Android phone will never reproduce.

caseStudies.title: web.dev: INP officially replaces FID (March 12, 2024)
caseStudies.body: Google's own announcement documents that as of March 12, 2024, Interaction to Next Paint became a stable Core Web Vital and First Input Delay was retired. The rationale, stated in the article, is that FID only measured the input delay of the first interaction and ignored event-handler processing and presentation, so many sites had 'good' FID yet still felt unresponsive. INP measures the full latency of interactions across the page lifetime, which is why sites with heavy JavaScript main-thread work often saw their responsiveness scores drop when the metric changed — an accurate, not pessimistic, reflection of the real experience.

caseStudies.title: Reserving dimensions to eliminate CLS (documented pattern)
caseStudies.body: web.dev's CLS guidance documents the canonical fix: setting explicit width and height attributes (or CSS aspect-ratio) on images and video, and reserving space for ad/embed slots, so the browser allocates the box before the resource loads and later content does not reflow. This is a well-documented general pattern rather than a single company result: it directly attacks CLS's root cause (unreserved space causing reflow) and is why modern frameworks like Next.js's <Image> component require or infer dimensions by default.

mcqs.q: As of 2024, which three metrics are the Core Web Vitals and their 'good' thresholds?
options: LCP ≤ 2.5s, FID ≤ 100ms, CLS ≤ 0.1
LCP ≤ 2.5s, CLS ≤ 0.1, INP ≤ 200ms
FCP ≤ 1.8s, TBT ≤ 200ms, CLS ≤ 0.25
LCP ≤ 4s, CLS ≤ 0.25, INP ≤ 500ms
mcqs.explanation: Since March 12, 2024, INP (≤200ms) replaced FID as the responsiveness Core Web Vital, joining LCP (≤2.5s) and CLS (≤0.1). The FID-based option is the pre-2024 set. The FCP/TBT option lists lab/diagnostic metrics, not Core Web Vitals. The last option lists the 'poor' thresholds, not 'good'.

mcqs.q: Why did Google replace FID with INP as the responsiveness metric?
options: INP is easier to measure in a lab than FID
FID only captured the input delay of the first interaction, ignoring handler processing time and all later interactions, so it overstated responsiveness
INP measures loading rather than responsiveness
FID could not be measured in the field
mcqs.explanation: FID measured only the delay before the first interaction's handler began — not how long the handler ran, and not any subsequent interaction — so pages could score well yet feel laggy. INP observes all interactions and their full latency (input delay + processing + presentation). Note INP is actually harder for labs to measure (there's no real user), which rules out the 'easier in a lab' option.

mcqs.q: A page shows a green Lighthouse (lab) score but is failing Core Web Vitals in Search Console. What is the most likely explanation?
options: Lighthouse is broken
Core Web Vitals are assessed on real users at the 75th percentile (field/CrUX data), which reflects slower real devices and networks that a single lab run does not
Search Console uses different thresholds than Lighthouse
The page must be re-submitted for indexing
mcqs.explanation: Vitals are field metrics from real users (CrUX), assessed at the 75th percentile split by device, so the slower quarter of real low-end mobile traffic counts — a fast lab machine won't reproduce it. Lighthouse also can't measure INP at all (it uses TBT as a proxy). The fix is to look at RUM/CrUX data, not the lab score.

mcqs.q: Your INP is poor at 380ms. Which change most directly targets the root cause?
options: Add width/height to all images
Break up long main-thread tasks and yield to the event loop so interactions can be handled and painted sooner
Preload the hero image
Move the stylesheet to the end of <body>
mcqs.explanation: INP is dominated by main-thread contention — long tasks delay input handling, processing, and the next paint. Breaking tasks and yielding (scheduler.yield/setTimeout/isInputPending) or offloading to a worker directly reduces that latency. Image dimensions target CLS, and preloading the hero targets LCP — different metrics.

mcqs.q: A hero banner loads via an ad script that injects markup after first paint, pushing the article down. Which vital degrades and why?
options: LCP, because the ad is the largest element
INP, because the ad handler is slow
CLS, because unreserved injected content reflows existing content, producing an unexpected layout shift
TTFB, because the ad server is slow
mcqs.explanation: Injecting content above existing content without reserving space causes the page to reflow — the definition of an unexpected layout shift, which CLS measures (impact × distance). The fix is to reserve the ad slot's dimensions ahead of time. TTFB isn't a Core Web Vital, and the symptom described is movement, not slow interaction or slow largest paint.

topics.name: HTTP Caching
topics.premise: HTTP caching lets a client or an intermediary store a server's response and reuse it for later equivalent requests, avoiding a network round-trip when the stored copy is still good enough. It has two complementary halves: freshness (is this copy still valid without asking the server?) governed mainly by Cache-Control, and validation (the copy may be stale, so cheaply confirm it with a conditional request) governed by ETag/If-None-Match and Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since, which the server answers with 304 Not Modified. Correctly configured, it is the single biggest lever on repeat-visit performance.
topics.year: HTTP caching has been part of the protocol since HTTP/1.1 (RFC 2068, 1997; RFC 2616, 1999). The current normative specification is RFC 9111 'HTTP Caching' (June 2022, STD 98), which obsoletes RFC 7234. Two widely used directives are defined outside RFC 9111: stale-while-revalidate/stale-if-error in RFC 5861 (2010) and immutable in RFC 8246 (2017).
topics.why: The network is the slowest, least reliable, and most expensive part of loading a web page: a request to origin costs a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake, a TLS handshake, and at least one round-trip of latency — often hundreds of milliseconds — before a single byte of the actual resource arrives, and it consumes bandwidth and server capacity every time. Yet most bytes a site serves (its JS bundles, CSS, images, fonts) do not change between two visits by the same user. Caching exists to exploit that: if the client already has a copy that is still good, the ideal outcome is to use it and touch the network zero times. When the client can't be sure the copy is still good, the second-best outcome is a conditional request — the client says 'I have version X, send me the body only if it changed,' and the server can answer with a tiny 304 (no body) if it hasn't. The whole design is a hierarchy of avoidance: avoid the network entirely when freshness lets you; when you can't, revalidate as cheaply as possible instead of re-downloading.
solutions: Cache-Control: max-age / s-maxage

max-age=N sets the freshness lifetime in seconds from the time the response was generated at the origin; while fresh, caches serve it with no network call. s-maxage overrides max-age for shared caches (CDNs/proxies) only, letting you cache longer at the edge than in the browser.
public vs private

public means any cache, including shared ones, may store the response (and permits storing responses that would otherwise be excluded, e.g. with Authorization). private restricts storage to a single-user (browser) cache — essential for personalized responses so a CDN never serves one user's data to another.
no-cache vs no-store

no-cache is a misnomer: the response MAY be stored, but MUST be revalidated with the origin before every reuse (good for content that changes unpredictably but is usually unchanged). no-store forbids storing the response anywhere at all — the correct directive for truly sensitive data.
must-revalidate

Once a stored response becomes stale, must-revalidate forbids serving it without successful revalidation — even if the origin is unreachable (in which case the cache must return an error, e.g. 504, rather than a stale copy). It closes the loophole where caches serve stale content when the origin is down.
ETag / If-None-Match (validation)

The server tags a response with an ETag (an opaque version identifier, often a content hash). On a conditional request the client sends If-None-Match: <etag>; if it still matches, the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body, saving the download. ETags are stronger than dates because they detect any change, including sub-second edits.
Last-Modified / If-Modified-Since (validation)

A weaker, timestamp-based validator: the server sends Last-Modified, the client echoes it in If-Modified-Since, and the server returns 304 if the resource hasn't changed since. Cheaper to compute than a hash but limited to 1-second granularity and unreliable for content that changes without a timestamp change.
immutable + stale-while-revalidate

immutable (RFC 8246) tells the browser a fresh response will not change, so it should skip revalidation even on reload — ideal for hashed assets. stale-while-revalidate=N (RFC 5861) lets a cache serve a stale copy instantly while it revalidates in the background, hiding revalidation latency from the user.
Cache-busting via hashed filenames

The dominant modern pattern: build tools emit assets like app.9f2a1c.js whose filename contains a content hash. Serve these with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable and cache them for a year; when the content changes the hash changes, so the URL changes, so the browser fetches a genuinely new file — cache invalidation without ever needing to invalidate.
topics.papers: RFC 9111 'HTTP Caching' (June 2022, STD 98) is the normative source for Cache-Control, freshness, validation, and shared vs private caches; it obsoletes RFC 7234. RFC 9110 'HTTP Semantics' defines conditional request headers (If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since) and the 304 status. Two extension RFCs define directives used in practice: RFC 5861 (stale-while-revalidate, stale-if-error) and RFC 8246 (immutable). MDN's HTTP caching guide and Google web.dev's caching guidance are the standard practitioner references.
topics.takeaway: Freshness (Cache-Control/max-age) lets you skip the network entirely; validation (ETag/Last-Modified → 304) lets you confirm a stale copy cheaply when you can't — so hash your immutable assets for a year and validate everything else.
topics.deepDive:
Reason from the cost of the network. Fetching a resource from origin means, in the worst case, DNS + TCP + TLS + at least one round-trip of latency before the first byte, plus bandwidth and server load — repeated on every request. But a returning user's browser usually already holds the exact bytes it needs. HTTP caching is the protocol's mechanism for exploiting that, and its two layers map directly onto two questions: 'can I reuse my copy without asking?' (freshness) and, failing that, 'can I confirm my copy cheaply?' (validation).

Freshness is a promise about time. When a response carries Cache-Control: max-age=3600, the origin is asserting the representation will be acceptable for the next hour, so any cache holding it may serve it with zero network contact until it becomes stale. max-age is measured from when the response was generated at the origin, and intermediary caches subtract the time the response has already spent aging (the Age header). s-maxage lets you tune shared caches (a CDN) independently of the browser. The public/private axis is orthogonal and about who may store: private confines a response to the end user's own cache — mandatory for personalized or authenticated content, because a shared CDN caching a private response would leak one user's data to the next.

The two 'no' directives are the most misunderstood in the spec. no-store is the strong one: nothing may be written to any cache — use it for sensitive data. no-cache does not mean 'don't cache'; it means 'you may store this, but you must revalidate with the origin before every reuse.' It is the right choice for a resource that rarely changes but must never be served stale (an HTML shell, a config file): the browser keeps the copy and, on each use, sends a conditional request that usually returns a tiny 304. must-revalidate hardens the stale case — normally a cache may sometimes serve stale content, but must-revalidate forbids reusing a stale response without a successful check, and if the origin is unreachable the cache must fail rather than serve stale.

Validation is what happens when freshness runs out. The server stamps responses with validators: an ETag, an opaque token (typically a content hash) that changes whenever the bytes change, and/or Last-Modified, a timestamp. When a cached copy goes stale, the client revalidates with a conditional request — If-None-Match: <etag> or If-Modified-Since: <date>. If nothing changed, the server returns 304 Not Modified with headers but no body, and the cache refreshes its copy's freshness and serves the stored bytes. This turns a potentially large download into a header-sized exchange. ETags are stronger than dates because they catch changes that don't move a second-granularity timestamp, but they cost the server a hash computation and must be consistent across a fleet of servers or they defeat themselves.

The headline pattern for modern frontends resolves the tension between 'cache aggressively' and 'ship updates instantly': cache-busting via content-hashed filenames. Build tools (webpack, Vite, esbuild, Next.js) emit files like main.4f8b2e.js whose name embeds a hash of the contents. Because the URL is unique to the content, you can safely serve it with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable — cache it for a year and never revalidate. When you deploy new code, the content changes, so the hash changes, so the URL changes, so the browser simply requests a different file. You get near-perfect caching of static assets and instant, atomic cache invalidation, without ETags or purges. The catch is that the HTML that references these files must NOT be cached this way — it must be revalidated (no-cache or a short max-age) so users pick up the new filenames; a common outage is serving stale HTML that points at deleted hashed bundles.

For system design, the model to hold is a layered cache and a spectrum of policies. The browser cache serves one user; shared caches (a CDN, a reverse proxy) serve many, which is why the private/public distinction and Vary correctness matter (a mis-negotiated Vary can cause a CDN to serve the wrong representation or fail to cache at all). The general strategy is: fingerprint immutable static assets and cache them for a year; put a short max-age or no-cache with an ETag on HTML and API responses that change; use stale-while-revalidate to hide revalidation latency on things that tolerate brief staleness; and reserve no-store for secrets. The failure modes are all forms of the same two mistakes — caching something that should be fresh (users see stale content, or a shared cache leaks private data) or not caching something that safely could be (needless round-trips and origin load). Getting it right is often the cheapest large performance win a frontend can ship.

caseStudies.title: Content-hashed assets + immutable (webpack/Vite/Next.js standard)
caseStudies.body: Modern build tooling emits JavaScript and CSS with a content hash in the filename (e.g. main.4f8b2e.js). Frameworks and hosts document serving these with Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable — a one-year lifetime with no revalidation — because the URL changes whenever the content does. This is a verifiable, near-universal production pattern (Next.js serves files under /_next/static with exactly this header, and Vite recommends the same). It achieves both maximal caching and instant, atomic invalidation, provided the referencing HTML is served with a short/revalidating cache policy so clients discover the new filenames.

caseStudies.title: 304 Not Modified via ETag (documented protocol behavior)
caseStudies.body: RFC 9110/9111 and MDN document the conditional-request flow: a server returns an ETag, the client stores it and, when its cached copy is stale, sends If-None-Match; if the resource is unchanged the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body. This is the mechanism CDNs and origin servers use to keep large but slowly-changing resources cheap to re-check — the client pays only for headers, not a full re-download, whenever the content hasn't actually changed.

mcqs.q: What does Cache-Control: no-cache actually instruct a cache to do?
options: Never store the response
Store the response but revalidate it with the origin before each reuse
Cache the response for zero seconds and delete it
Store only in shared caches
mcqs.explanation: no-cache is a misnomer: the response MAY be stored, but it MUST be revalidated (via a conditional request) before it is reused. The directive that forbids storing entirely is no-store. Reason from the spec's freshness/validation split — no-cache disables freshness reuse, not storage.

mcqs.q: You serve a user's personalized account page from behind a CDN. Which Cache-Control setting is correct?
options: public, max-age=31536000, immutable
private (or no-store), so a shared CDN never stores and re-serves it to another user
public, max-age=0
s-maxage=86400
mcqs.explanation: Personalized content must not be stored in a shared cache, or one user's data could be served to another. private confines it to the browser cache; no-store prevents any storage if it's sensitive. All the 'public'/s-maxage options explicitly permit shared caches to store it — a data-leak bug.

mcqs.q: Which is the fundamental difference between freshness and validation?
options: Freshness uses ETags; validation uses max-age
Freshness reuses a copy without contacting the origin; validation contacts the origin to confirm a stale copy, ideally getting a bodyless 304
Freshness applies only to CDNs; validation only to browsers
They are two names for the same mechanism
mcqs.explanation: Freshness (governed by max-age/expires) lets a cache serve a copy with zero network calls while it's still fresh. Validation (ETag/If-None-Match, Last-Modified/If-Modified-Since) is the fallback once stale: a cheap conditional request that returns 304 if unchanged. The whole design is 'avoid the network; if you can't, revalidate cheaply.'

mcqs.q: Why can hashed filenames (main.4f8b2e.js) safely be served with max-age=31536000, immutable?
options: Because a year is the maximum allowed max-age
Because the filename encodes a content hash, so any content change produces a different URL — the cached URL never needs invalidating
Because immutable disables the browser cache
Because JavaScript files never change
mcqs.explanation: The URL is unique to the content. If the file changes, its hash and therefore its URL change, so the browser requests a genuinely different file — you never need to invalidate the old URL. This gives maximal caching plus atomic invalidation, as long as the HTML referencing these files is itself revalidated so clients pick up new filenames.

mcqs.q: After a deploy, some users see a broken page: their HTML references JS bundles that 404. What is the most likely caching misconfiguration?
options: The JS bundles were served with no-store
The HTML document was cached with a long immutable max-age, so users kept old HTML pointing at hashed bundles that no longer exist
The ETag was too long
stale-while-revalidate was enabled on the images
mcqs.explanation: Hashed bundles should be immutable and long-lived, but the HTML that references them must be revalidated (no-cache or short max-age) so clients discover new filenames. If the HTML itself is cached aggressively, users hold stale HTML pointing at deleted bundles — a classic deploy outage. The asset caching is fine; the HTML policy is the bug.

topics.name: Content Negotiation
topics.premise: Content negotiation is the HTTP mechanism by which a single URL can serve different representations of the same resource — a different media type, compression, language, or image format — chosen to best fit the requesting client. In the dominant server-driven (proactive) form, the client advertises its preferences via request headers like Accept, Accept-Encoding, and Accept-Language, and the server picks a representation. The server then emits a Vary header naming which request headers influenced the choice, so caches can store and reuse each representation correctly.
topics.year: Content negotiation is a core HTTP/1.1 feature, present since RFC 2068 (1997) and RFC 2616 (1999). Its current normative definition is RFC 9110 'HTTP Semantics' (June 2022, STD 97), which formalizes proactive vs reactive negotiation, the Accept-* headers, quality values, and Vary; it obsoletes RFC 7231. The modern evolution — Client Hints (Sec-CH-* request headers, opted into via Accept-CH) — is specified by the HTTP Client Hints infrastructure in RFC 8942 (2021), with device/UA hints developed in W3C/WICG work since ~2020.
topics.why: The web has one namespace — URLs — but clients are wildly heterogeneous: different browsers support different image codecs and compression algorithms, users speak different languages, devices have different screen densities and widths, and networks have different costs. You could solve this with different URLs per variant (image.avif vs image.webp vs image.jpg), but that fragments links, breaks sharing, complicates the HTML, and forces the author to know every client's capabilities in advance. Content negotiation keeps a single canonical URL and pushes the selection into the protocol: the client, which alone knows its own capabilities, declares them, and the server, which alone knows what representations exist, selects. The catch is that caching assumes a URL maps to one response; if a URL can return different bytes depending on request headers, a shared cache could serve the wrong variant (a Brotli body to a client that can't decode it, or the French page to an English user). The Vary header exists precisely to make negotiation and caching coexist: it tells caches which request headers are part of the cache key.
solutions: Accept (media-type negotiation)

The client lists media types it can handle, with optional q-values (0–1) ranking preference: Accept: text/html,application/xhtml+xml,application/xml;q=0.9,*/*;q=0.8. The server selects the best available representation, or returns 406 Not Acceptable if it can satisfy none.
Accept-Encoding (compression negotiation)

The client advertises supported content codings — Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, zstd — and the server compresses with the best mutually supported one, echoing its choice in Content-Encoding. Brotli (br) usually beats gzip on text; zstd is a newer high-ratio option. This is transparent to the URL and hugely reduces transfer size.
Accept-Language (language negotiation)

Accept-Language: en-US,en;q=0.9,fr;q=0.8 lets the server pick a localized representation. q-values express fallbacks (prefer en-US, then any English, then French). Useful, but many sites still prefer explicit locale in the URL for shareability and SEO.
Image-format negotiation via Accept

Browsers send format preferences in the image request's Accept header, e.g. Accept: image/avif,image/webp,image/*,*/*;q=0.8. A server or image CDN inspects it and returns AVIF to browsers that support it, WebP to the next tier, and JPEG/PNG as fallback — all from one URL, saving large amounts of bytes without markup changes.
The Vary response header

Vary lists the request headers that affected representation selection (e.g. Vary: Accept-Encoding, Accept-Language). Caches must include those headers in their cache key, so a gzip body is only served to gzip-capable clients. Vary: * or an over-broad Vary (e.g. on the full User-Agent) fragments the cache so badly it effectively disables caching.
Client Hints (Sec-CH-* — the evolution)

Client Hints move device/context signals out of the ever-parsed User-Agent string into explicit, opt-in request headers. The server advertises what it wants via Accept-CH (e.g. Accept-CH: Sec-CH-DPR, Sec-CH-Width, Sec-CH-Viewport-Width); the browser then sends Sec-CH-DPR: 2, Sec-CH-Width: 600, etc., letting the server return correctly sized/DPR-scaled images. These supersede the earlier unprefixed DPR/Width hints.
Server-driven (proactive) vs agent-driven (reactive)

Proactive: the client sends preference headers and the server chooses in one round-trip (the common case). Reactive: the server returns a list of alternatives (e.g. 300 Multiple Choices) and the user agent picks, costing an extra round-trip but giving the client full control. Nearly all real-world negotiation is proactive; reactive is rare because of the round-trip cost and lack of a standard selection UI.
Interaction with CDNs and caching

On a CDN, correct Vary is essential: too narrow and clients get the wrong variant; too broad (User-Agent) and the hit rate collapses. Best practice is to negotiate on a small, low-cardinality set (Accept-Encoding, sometimes Accept for images) and to normalize headers at the edge so the cache key stays small.
topics.papers: RFC 9110 'HTTP Semantics' (June 2022, STD 97) is the normative reference: Section 12 defines proactive vs reactive content negotiation, the Accept, Accept-Encoding, and Accept-Language header fields, quality values, and the Vary response header (obsoletes RFC 7231). Client Hints infrastructure is defined in RFC 8942 (HTTP Client Hints, 2021), with UA and device hints in W3C/WICG specifications. MDN's Content negotiation guide and the Vary and Accept-CH reference pages are the standard practitioner documentation.
topics.takeaway: One URL should return the best representation for each client; the client advertises capabilities via Accept-* headers, the server chooses, and the Vary header keeps caches from serving the wrong variant.
topics.deepDive: The problem content negotiation solves comes from a tension baked into the web: URLs are meant to be stable, shareable identifiers of a resource, but clients are radically diverse in what bytes they can actually use. A modern Chrome build decodes AVIF and speaks Brotli and zstd; a decade-old browser needs JPEG and gzip; a phone has a 3x display and a 400px-wide viewport; a user reads Japanese. You could mint a URL per combination, but that explodes the link space, breaks caching and sharing, and forces the HTML author to encode capability knowledge they don't have. Negotiation instead keeps the canonical URL and lets the two parties who actually hold the relevant knowledge cooperate: the client, which alone knows its capabilities and preferences, and the server, which alone knows which representations exist. The common mechanism is server-driven (proactive) negotiation. The client sends preference headers — Accept for media types, Accept-Encoding for compression, Accept-Language for language — each optionally weighted with quality values from 0 to 1 that express ranked fallbacks rather than hard requirements. Accept-Encoding: gzip, br, zstd says 'I can decode any of these,' and the server responds with whatever it supports best, announcing the choice in Content-Encoding. If the server can satisfy none of the client's Accept media types it may return 406 Not Acceptable, though in practice servers usually fall back to a default rather than fail. The most visible modern use is image-format negotiation, and it is elegant precisely because it needs no markup. When a browser requests an image it sends something like Accept: image/avif,image/webp,image/*,*/*;q=0.8. An image CDN or server reads that single header and returns AVIF to clients that accept it, WebP to the next tier, and JPEG/PNG otherwise — all behind one . This can cut image bytes dramatically (AVIF and WebP are far smaller than JPEG at equal quality) without the author writing a element with per-format sources. It is a clean demonstration of the first principle: one URL, best representation, chosen by the party that knows. The hard part is caching, and it is where most real-world bugs live. A cache's core assumption is that a URL identifies one response. Negotiation violates that: the same URL can legitimately return a Brotli body or an identity body, an English page or a French one. If a shared cache (a CDN) stored the first response it saw and served it to everyone, it would hand a Brotli-encoded body to a client that only sent Accept-Encoding: gzip — a corrupt page. The Vary response header repairs this by extending the cache key: Vary: Accept-Encoding tells every cache that the response varies by that request header, so it must store and match per encoding. Getting Vary right is a balancing act: omit a header you negotiated on and caches serve wrong variants; include a high-cardinality header (the classic mistake is Vary: User-Agent, which has millions of distinct values) and you shatter the cache into near-unique entries, destroying the hit rate. The discipline is to negotiate on the smallest, lowest-cardinality set possible and normalize those headers at the edge. Client Hints are the negotiation model's evolution, born from the failure of the User-Agent string. Historically, servers sniffed the ever-growing, unreliable User-Agent to guess device density and width for responsive images — brittle and privacy-hostile. Client Hints replace this with explicit, opt-in headers: the server advertises what it wants via Accept-CH (e.g. Accept-CH: Sec-CH-DPR, Sec-CH-Width, Sec-CH-Viewport-Width), and only then does the browser send Sec-CH-DPR: 2 and Sec-CH-Width: 600 on subsequent requests, letting the server return an image scaled to the exact device pixel ratio and layout width. The Sec- prefix marks them as browser-controlled headers that page script cannot forge, and they supersede the earlier unprefixed DPR/Width hints. Because they participate in negotiation, hint headers must also be listed in Vary (or handled via the Critical-CH mechanism) to keep caches correct — and because they can be used for fingerprinting, they are deliberately opt-in and gated. There is also reactive (agent-driven) negotiation, where the server returns a list of alternatives (conceptually a 300 Multiple Choices) and lets the user agent pick. It is almost never used in practice: it costs an extra round-trip and there is no standardized machine-readable format for the choice list, so proactive negotiation dominates. For frontend system design, the practical guidance is: rely on proactive negotiation for compression (nearly free wins with Brotli) and image format (large wins via an image CDN); prefer explicit locale in URLs over Accept-Language when SEO and shareability matter; use Client Hints for responsive images when you control the server/CDN; and treat Vary as part of your caching contract — negotiate narrowly, set Vary precisely, and never vary on User-Agent. The recurring failure mode across all of these is a mismatch between what you negotiated on and what your Vary/cache key says, which either corrupts responses or collapses your cache hit rate.

caseStudies.title: AVIF/WebP delivery via the Accept header (image CDNs)
caseStudies.body: Image CDNs and frameworks (e.g. Cloudflare Images, Cloudinary, Next.js Image Optimization) implement documented content negotiation on the request's Accept header: they inspect image/avif and image/webp tokens and return the smallest format the client supports from a single URL, falling back to JPEG/PNG. Because AVIF and WebP are substantially smaller than JPEG at equivalent quality (web.dev documents typical WebP savings around 25–35% over comparable JPEG), this yields large real transfer savings with no markup changes — provided the response sets Vary: Accept so caches don't serve AVIF to a client that can't decode it.

caseStudies.title: The Vary: User-Agent anti-pattern
caseStudies.body: A well-documented caching pitfall (covered by MDN and CDN vendor docs) is setting Vary: User-Agent to serve device-specific responses. Because the User-Agent string has effectively unbounded cardinality, the CDN creates a near-unique cache entry per request, collapsing the hit rate and hammering the origin. The documented remedy is to negotiate on low-cardinality signals instead — Client Hints (Sec-CH-DPR/Sec-CH-Width) or a normalized device class — and to keep Vary limited to headers with few distinct values such as Accept-Encoding.

mcqs.q: What is the primary purpose of the Vary response header in content negotiation?
options: To compress the response body
To tell caches which request headers were used to select the representation, so they form the cache key correctly
To list the languages a server supports
To force the client to revalidate on every request
mcqs.explanation: Negotiation means one URL can return different bytes depending on request headers, which breaks a cache's URL-to-response assumption. Vary names the request headers that influenced selection so caches key on them and never serve, say, a Brotli body to a gzip-only client. It's about cache correctness, not compression or revalidation.

mcqs.q: A browser fetches an and the server returns AVIF from the same URL that also serves JPEG. How did the server know to send AVIF?
options: It parsed the User-Agent string
The browser included image/avif in the request's Accept header, and the server selected the best supported format
The URL ended in .avif
The browser sent Accept-Encoding: avif
mcqs.explanation: Browsers advertise image-format support in the Accept header of image requests (e.g. Accept: image/avif,image/webp,*/*). The server negotiates on that and returns the smallest supported format from one URL. Format is a media type (Accept), not a content coding (Accept-Encoding), and no per-format URL is needed.

mcqs.q: Why are Client Hints (Sec-CH-DPR, Sec-CH-Width) considered an improvement over sniffing the User-Agent for responsive images?
options: They are sent on every request automatically with no server involvement
They are explicit, opt-in (via Accept-CH), low-cardinality, browser-controlled headers, unlike the unreliable high-cardinality User-Agent
They compress images automatically
They eliminate the need for a Vary header
mcqs.explanation: User-Agent sniffing is brittle, privacy-hostile, and high-cardinality (bad for caches). Client Hints are opt-in (the server must request them via Accept-CH), carry a single clear signal, and the Sec- prefix means page script can't forge them. They still must be reflected in Vary/Critical-CH for cache correctness, so the 'eliminate Vary' option is wrong.

mcqs.q: A CDN sets Vary: User-Agent to deliver device-specific pages. What is the likely consequence?
options: Perfect cache hit rate
The cache fragments into near-unique entries because User-Agent has enormous cardinality, collapsing the hit rate and increasing origin load
Clients receive corrupted, wrongly-encoded bodies
The origin stops receiving requests entirely
mcqs.explanation: Vary extends the cache key with the named header's value. User-Agent has effectively unbounded distinct values, so almost every request becomes a unique key — the cache barely hits and the origin is hammered. The fix is to vary on low-cardinality signals (Accept-Encoding, Client Hints, or a normalized device class).

mcqs.q: Nearly all real-world content negotiation is server-driven (proactive) rather than agent-driven (reactive). Why?
options: Reactive negotiation is forbidden by RFC 9110
Reactive negotiation needs an extra round-trip and has no standard machine-readable format for the client to pick from, so proactive (one round-trip, client advertises prefs) is far more practical
Proactive negotiation does not require any request headers
Reactive negotiation cannot be cached at all
mcqs.explanation: In reactive negotiation the server returns a list of alternatives and the client makes a second request to fetch the chosen one — an extra round-trip — and there's no standardized selection format, so it's rarely automated. Proactive negotiation resolves in a single round-trip using the Accept-* headers the client already sends, which is why it dominates.

topics.name: Lazy Loading
topics.premise: Lazy loading is the deliberate deferral of loading a resource until it is actually needed — typically until it enters (or nears) the viewport, or until a route/interaction demands its code. It applies to images and iframes (via the native loading="lazy" attribute), to arbitrary DOM/media (via IntersectionObserver), and to JavaScript itself (via dynamic import()). The goal is to shrink the critical path: fetch, parse, and render only what the user can currently see, and pay for the rest on demand.
topics.year: The pattern predates any spec — developers hand-rolled scroll-based image deferral throughout the 2000s. IntersectionObserver was incubated by the W3C Web Performance Working Group and shipped in Chrome 51 (2016), reaching cross-browser support by ~2019. Native loading="lazy" for images landed in Chrome 76 (2019) and is now standardized in the HTML Living Standard; iframe support and broad browser coverage (including Safari 16.4, 2023) followed. Dynamic import() was standardized in ECMAScript 2020.
topics.why: The browser's critical rendering path is bounded by network round-trips, bytes on the wire, and main-thread work (parse, compile, layout, paint). Every resource referenced eagerly competes for the same finite connection pool and CPU, delaying first paint and interactivity. A long article may reference 40 images, but a phone viewport shows two or three above the fold; eagerly fetching all 40 wastes bandwidth on pixels the user may never scroll to, and pushes the truly-visible content behind them in the request queue. The same holds for JavaScript: a single monolithic bundle forces the engine to download and compile code for routes the user hasn't visited. First principles: the user's device has a fixed budget of network and CPU per unit time, so anything you load that isn't yet visible is directly stealing from what is.
solutions: Native loading="lazy"
Add loading="lazy" to and
IntersectionObserver for custom lazy

For non-image content (background images, embeds, analytics beacons, animations), instantiate new IntersectionObserver(callback, {rootMargin, threshold}). It fires the callback off the main-thread's synchronous path when a target's intersection with the root (viewport by default) crosses a threshold, replacing scroll+getBoundingClientRect() polling that caused layout thrash.
rootMargin to pre-load early

Set rootMargin: '200px 0px' so the observer fires before the element is visible, giving the fetch time to complete during scroll. This trades a little eagerness for the elimination of visible pop-in — the mechanism's central tuning knob.
unobserve after trigger

In the callback, once entry.isIntersecting is true, swap data-src → src (or import the module), then call observer.unobserve(entry.target). One-shot lazy load avoids repeated callbacks and lets the observer be garbage-collected once all targets fire.
Route-based code splitting

Load each route's JS on navigation via dynamic import() (React.lazy + Suspense, Vue defineAsyncComponent, or a framework router). The initial bundle carries only the shell and the first route; other routes are separate chunks fetched when reached.
Component-based / interaction lazy

Defer heavy widgets (rich text editors, charts, maps, modals) behind import() triggered by an interaction or IntersectionObserver. A 300 KB editor that 5% of users open should not sit in the initial bundle for the other 95%.
Reserve space to prevent CLS

Always set width/height (or aspect-ratio, or a sized skeleton) on lazy media. A deferred image with no reserved box collapses to zero height, then pushes content down when it loads — a layout shift that inflates CLS. Reserving the box makes the load invisible to layout.
Never lazy-load the LCP element

The hero/above-the-fold image is almost always the Largest Contentful Paint element. loading="lazy" on it delays its fetch behind layout, regressing LCP. Load it eagerly (loading="eager") and ideally fetchpriority="high"; reserve lazy strictly for below-the-fold.
topics.papers: The authoritative reference for native lazy loading is the WHATWG HTML Living Standard's lazy loading attributes section (the loading attribute on img and iframe). IntersectionObserver is specified by the W3C Intersection Observer specification (v1 CR, with v2 adding trackVisibility). Dynamic import() is defined in the ECMAScript specification (import() call syntax, ES2020). web.dev's Core Web Vitals documentation is the canonical source for the LCP (<= 2.5s good, at the 75th percentile) and CLS (<= 0.1 good) thresholds that lazy loading must respect.
topics.takeaway: Don't pay for what the user can't yet see — defer below-the-fold media and off-route code, but always reserve layout space (or you trade LCP wins for CLS losses) and never lazy-load the LCP element itself.
topics.deepDive:
Start from the physical constraints. A browser opens a limited number of connections per origin (HTTP/1.1 caps ~6; HTTP/2 multiplexes over one but still shares finite bandwidth), and the main thread can only parse, compile, and execute so much JavaScript per millisecond. Every byte you request eagerly is a byte that isn't available for the content the user is looking at right now. Lazy loading is simply the discipline of aligning what you fetch with what is currently needed — nothing more exotic than that.

For images and iframes, the native loading="lazy" attribute is the right primitive because the browser knows things your JavaScript cannot: the true scroll position, the effective connection type, and how the preload scanner is prioritizing the rest of the document. Its distance-from-viewport threshold is adaptive — on a slow connection it starts fetching earlier to hide latency. Because it is declarative, it works before your JS runs and cannot be defeated by a hydration delay. The cost is that you surrender fine control; when you need to lazy-load a CSS background, an embed, an animation, or to fire an analytics event on visibility, you drop down to IntersectionObserver.

IntersectionObserver exists precisely to kill the old scroll-handler pattern. The pre-2016 approach attached a scroll listener and called getBoundingClientRect() on every element on every scroll tick — each call forcing a synchronous layout, producing jank. The observer instead lets the browser compute intersections asynchronously, off the synchronous rendering path, and only invokes your callback when a configured threshold is crossed. You tune two knobs: threshold (what fraction of the target must be visible) and rootMargin (an inflation of the root box, so you can begin loading, say, 200px before the element scrolls into view). The idiomatic lazy-load reads entry.isIntersecting, swaps a data-src placeholder to the real src, then calls unobserve so the element stops being watched and the machinery can be collected.

Code lazy loading is the same principle applied to the most expensive resource of all: JavaScript, which must be downloaded, parsed, and compiled before it can run. Dynamic import() returns a promise for a module and signals the bundler to emit that module as a separate chunk. Route-based splitting (React.lazy behind Suspense, framework routers) means the initial download contains only the shell plus the landing route; navigating fetches the next chunk. Component-based splitting defers heavy, rarely-used widgets behind an interaction. The trade-off is a fetch waterfall: split too finely and a click triggers a chain of round-trips before anything renders, so pair lazy chunks with prefetching (e.g. on link hover or when the route becomes likely) to hide the latency.

The dominant failure mode ties directly into another Core Web Vital: layout shift. A lazily loaded image with no intrinsic dimensions occupies zero height until it arrives, then suddenly reflows everything below it — a jarring jump that Cumulative Layout Shift measures as impact-fraction times distance-fraction, with a 'good' budget of 0.1 or less at the 75th percentile. The fix is to reserve the box up front: set width and height attributes (which modern browsers turn into an aspect-ratio) or render a correctly sized skeleton, so the load fills a slot that already existed and the page never moves. Placeholders (LQIP/BlurHash, solid color, skeleton) additionally smooth the perceived experience.

The sharpest and most common mistake is lazy-loading the very element you most need fast: the hero image, which is usually the LCP element. Marking it loading="lazy" pushes its fetch behind layout and behind the viewport-proximity check, adding hundreds of milliseconds to LCP whose 'good' threshold is 2.5s at the 75th percentile. The correct policy is a split strategy: above-the-fold, load eagerly and hint fetchpriority="high" (and preload if it's discovered late); below-the-fold, lazy-load with reserved space. In a system-design interview, articulate lazy loading as this budget-allocation decision — not 'add loading=lazy everywhere', but 'defer everything the user can't see, protect the things they can, and never let the deferral cause a shift.'
